name: Mesh
baseline: jemalloc (Firefox, Redis) and glibc malloc (SPEC CPU2006, Ruby)
workload: Heap size over time for Firefox 57 Speedometer, Redis 4.0.2 insertion/defrag test, SPECint 2006, Ruby microbenchmark.
claimed_speedup: Reduces Firefox mean heap by 16% vs jemalloc and Redis by 39%; 400.perlbench peak RSS 564 MB vs 664 MB glibc, 614 MB jemalloc, 732 MB Hoard (15% below glibc); SPECint geomean memory -2.4% and runtime +0.7% vs glibc; 3.9% runtime overhead on perlbench
compiler_and_flags: SPEC built with clang 4.0 -O2; Mesh built with gcc 8 -O3 -flto
hardware: MacBook Pro, Intel i7-5600U, 16 GiB RAM, Linux 4.18 Ubuntu Bionic
tradeoffs: Drop-in malloc replacement for Linux and macOS (Windows in development); trades small runtime overhead (up to 10.7% on the Ruby microbenchmark with randomization) for memory savings; relies on virtual-memory page remapping.
caveats: Benefit is memory footprint, not speed; runtime is equal or slightly slower. Paper numbers from 2019 on old software versions (jemalloc 3.6.0, glibc 2.26). Paper PDF read from the repo; benchmark scripts not in a dedicated directory, so reproducibility is partial.
found_via: GitHub: pool arena allocator garbage collector faster than malloc Boehm GC benchmark; direct fetch of plasma-umass/Mesh and its PDF

name: SGCL
workload: Single-operation costs: pointer copy and object allocation in a concurrent GC library versus shared_ptr and malloc.
claimed_speedup: Allocation 2.8 ns vs malloc 17 ns; pointer copy 1.4 ns onto the stack and 1.8 ns into an object vs shared_ptr 4.7 ns alone and 100-300 ns on a shared object (Apple M2 Ultra)
hardware: Apple M2 Ultra, Apple clang (flags not stated)
tradeoffs: Header-only C++20 concurrent non-moving generational mark-and-sweep collector with no stop-the-world phase; uses extra cores for the collector; README now covers a whole application platform (net, crypto, codecs).
caveats: First-party numbers on one machine, flags and benchmark code not stated; platform testing is Apple Silicon only, Linux and Windows pending. Does not compare with Boehm GC in the README. Allocation cost excludes collector work on other cores.
found_via: GitHub: C++ garbage collector library faster than Boehm GC (WebSearch), README of pebal/sgcl

name: Bloodmoon001/memory-allocator
workload: Google Benchmark micro-benchmarks: single int alloc+free, std::string create+destroy, 10,000 bulk allocations, ops/s throughput for a fixed-size pool allocator.
claimed_speedup: Single int alloc+free 2,731 ns vs 29,067 ns (10.6x); std::string 7,240 vs 19,826 ns (2.7x); 10,000 bulk allocs 54,860 vs 433,902 ns (7.9x); 188M vs 23M ops/s (8.1x)
tradeoffs: Header-only C++17 fixed-size pool with intrusive free list, O(1) alloc/free; single-size slots only, not a general allocator; likely not thread-safe.
caveats: Windows MSVC malloc baseline is slow; benchmark in benchmarks/bench_allocator.cpp but numbers come from the README, not rerun; pool versus general malloc is not like for like. Thread-safety not confirmed.
found_via: WebSearch: arena allocator C++ header-only faster than malloc

name: obstack (cleeus)
workload: Allocate and deallocate 514,000 ops totalling 1 GB (single thread) and 538,000/540,000 ops on two/four threads.
claimed_speedup: Single thread: obstack 272 ms vs malloc/free 26,882 ms vs new/delete 27,654 ms; 4 threads: 125 ms vs 108,245 ms (malloc/free)
tradeoffs: Pointer-bump memory arena; frees whole arena at once, not per-object free; C++ API.
caveats: Arena versus general malloc, different semantics; 2012-era hardware and compiler; benchmark allocation pattern favours bump allocation; abandoned since 2015.
found_via: WebSearch: arena allocator C++ header-only faster than malloc

name: fast-alloc
workload: Pool, stack and free-list allocators benchmarked against new/delete and malloc on Linux, macOS and Windows.
claimed_speedup: Linux: pool 3.0x vs new/delete, stack 2.4x alloc/reset and 11.9x frame ops, free list 1.0x vs malloc; macOS: pool 4.0x, stack 4.7x; Windows MSVC: pool 14.9x, stack 20.1x
hardware: AMD Ryzen 7 PRO 8700GE (Linux); Apple ARM64 (macOS); MSVC 19.51 (Windows)
tradeoffs: C++20 pool, stack and free-list allocators; specialised allocators, not a general malloc replacement.
caveats: First-party README table only; the free-list allocator ties malloc (1.0x); the Windows ratios mostly reflect a slow MSVC baseline; four commits co-authored with GitHub Copilot.
found_via: WebSearch: C++ memory pool allocator fixed-size benchmark vs malloc

name: ArenaAllocator (privateMwb)
workload: 1M-iteration benchmarks of a fixed-capacity bump arena versus a new[]-based stdArena: capacity-failure path, reset and refill, large and over-aligned allocations.
claimed_speedup: Reset + refill 101.67 ms vs 14.16 s (~139x); large allocation 680.08 us vs 1.27 ms (~1.9x); over-aligned 770.38 us vs 1.27 ms (~1.6x); failure path 308.34 us vs 1.76 s
compiler_and_flags: Release build, C++20 (flags not stated in README)
hardware: not stated on page (benchmarks/baselines/v1.0.0.json reportedly has environment)
tradeoffs: Header-only fixed-capacity bump-pointer arena with frame rollback; capacity fixed at construction; no per-object free.
caveats: The baseline is the author's own naive stdArena, not malloc or a known incumbent; the big ratios come from comparing an O(1) reset with per-object new/delete. I did not open the baseline JSON.
found_via: WebSearch: arena allocator C++ header-only faster than malloc

name: halloc
workload: GPU dynamic allocation: 16-byte allocations by tens of thousands of threads with more than 100 MiB allocated on K20X.
claimed_speedup: More than 1.5 billion mallocs/s (more than 1 billion malloc/free pairs/s) on K20X with 16-byte allocations
tradeoffs: Slab allocator using bit arrays and hashing for GPUs; Kepler only, Maxwell unsupported; no resize after init; allocations above 3 KiB fall back to CUDA allocator.
caveats: README gives the throughput number but no comparison table in the repo (the claim of beating other GPU allocators is in the author's paper, not opened); abandoned since 2015; GPL.
found_via: WebSearch: GPU memory allocator pool CUDA faster than cudaMalloc benchmark
